fixes.explanation: That's the request. The people ask Ezra to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, "…which the LORD had commanded for Israel." They're asking for the Book, and I love that for them.

Good guess, friend, but the text never has them ask for the ark. It says they asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses. Ezra is a scribe, so I'd say a book is right up his alley. The whole crowd wants the Word itself.
I get it, mail is exciting. But the text says the crowd asked for the Book of the Law of Moses, not any letters. They gathered in the square for the Word the LORD had commanded for Israel.
Not quite, friend. The text says Ezra read from daybreak until noon. So noon is where that reading stopped, not where it started. The people were already listening back at daybreak.
The text has no night shift here. It says Ezra read aloud from daybreak until noon. That's a morning, a long one, but still a morning.
False is right. The text says "…all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law." That's every single person, for hours.
No turning away in this square. As Ezra opens the book, all the people stand up. He opened it in full view of all the people, since he was standing above them all.
Copying is serious work, but that's not what the text says here. The Law was read and explained, "giving insight," so the people could understand. The goal in that square was understanding.
False is right. Nehemiah says, "Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared…" He sends them to the table, not away from it.

Portions! Nehemiah says to "…send out portions to those who have nothing prepared…" He puts that right alongside the eating and drinking. So the feast comes with a gift for people who have nothing prepared.
A messenger would be handy, but that's not what Nehemiah says. He tells the people to send out portions to those who have nothing prepared. The portions are the gift.
That's the line. Nehemiah says, "Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength." The strength he names is the joy of the LORD.
Good thinking, friend. But on this day, Nehemiah doesn't point to the wall. He says, "…the joy of the LORD is your strength." The strength he names is the joy of the LORD.

Understandable, but that's not what Nehemiah says. He tells them, "Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength." The strength he names is the joy of the LORD. That's a relief for anyone who's ever been tired.

Good thinking, friend. But the text gives a different reason for the rejoicing here. It says they rejoiced "…because they understood the words that had been made known to them." This party was about the Word.
Nothing in this passage says that. The text tells us why they rejoiced greatly: "…because they understood the words that had been made known to them." The reason it gives is understanding.
Planning is a good habit, but the text gives a different reason. The family heads, priests and Levites gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. Studying is the reason it gives.
Good guess, friend. The text gives a different reason, though. They gathered around Ezra the scribe "…to study the words of the Law."

Branches! The message says, "Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written." Those are the materials, straight from the hill country.
Stones would make a solid house, I'll give you that. But the message says to bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees. The booths come from branches, not stones.

False is right. The text says the people made booths "…on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim." The courts of the house of God are only one of those places. Booths went up on rooftops, in courtyards and in the squares too.

David is a famous name, but the text doesn't mention him here. It says, "From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this." Joshua is the name the text gives.

Solomon is a big name, but this verse doesn't mention him. The text says, "From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this." Joshua is the name it gives.

Only the first day? That'd be a one-batch bakery, friend, and I don't run one of those. The text says, "Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God." The reading didn't stop after day one. It kept going all the way through the feast.
